raw_source.coverage_limit: This is not a claim of reading the whole book. Source use sites listed below are the use sites actually encountered on these pages.

global_domains_quantifiers_and_definitio.fact: Throughout the book, n is a fixed positive integer greater than 1; Omega is an open nonempty subset of R^n.
global_domains_quantifiers_and_definitio.consequence_for_reading: The source Theorem 1.4 is read under n > 1. These pages do not state it for dimensions zero or one.

global_domains_quantifiers_and_definitio.fact: A complex-valued C^2 function u on Omega is harmonic when Delta u = 0. Delta is the sum of second partial derivatives in the real Euclidean coordinate variables.
For a set E in R^n that need not be open, harmonicity on E means that u admits a harmonic extension to an open set containing E.
global_domains_quantifiers_and_definitio.consequence_for_reading: Harmonicity on a closed ball in 1.4 and 1.6 is a neighborhood-extension hypothesis, not merely interior harmonicity plus a specified boundary value.

global_domains_quantifiers_and_definitio.fact: Functions are complex valued unless explicitly stated otherwise. C^k(Omega), C^infinity(Omega), and C(E) are defined by continuous differentiability and continuity; C(E) allows E to be an arbitrary subset. Real-valued restrictions are expressly stated where used.
The norm is Euclidean. B(a,r) is {x in R^n : |x-a| < r}; its closure is the closed ball. B denotes the unit ball, sometimes B_n to emphasize dimension. S is the boundary of B, hence the unit sphere.
global_domains_quantifiers_and_definitio.radius_reading: The source uses r as a radius and subsequent applications explicitly choose r > 0; Theorem 1.4 does not separately print a quantified r > 0 clause. A zero or negative radius case is not supplied by the source wording.

pins.location: Translation and beginning of dilation definition

global_domains_quantifiers_and_definitio.fact: Translations preserve harmonicity. For r > 0, u_r(x)=u(rx) is defined on (1/r)Omega and satisfies Delta(u_r)=r^2(Delta u)_r, so positive dilates preserve harmonicity. Orthogonal composition also preserves harmonicity.
global_domains_quantifiers_and_definitio.use: The normalization to B in 1.4 and 1.6 has this source context.

measure_and_law_conventions.fact: sigma is normalized surface-area measure on S, with sigma(S)=1. It is characterized as the unique Borel probability measure on S invariant under every orthogonal transformation: sigma(T(E))=sigma(E) for every Borel E subset S.
measure_and_law_conventions.scope: The measure is stated on S. These pages do not define an implementation-specific ambient measure, subtype measure, or pushforward construction.

measure_and_law_conventions.fact: V=V_n is Lebesgue volume measure on R^n, whereas s is surface-area measure on the relevant boundary. Green identities use unnormalized ds, not d sigma. D_n denotes the outward-unit-normal derivative, not a numbered coordinate derivative in these formulas.

S_n is the unit sphere in ambient R^n; s_n and sigma_n denote unnormalized and normalized surface-area measures on it. The footnote contrasts S_n with the common notation S^(n-1), explaining that S_n emphasizes ambient dimension.
measure_and_law_conventions.regularity_of_exposition: The appendix explicitly presumes familiarity with surface-area measure and warns that some following arguments are intuitive rather than fully rigorous.

measure_and_law_conventions.fact: A.2 states s_n(S_n)=n V_n(B_n). Its displayed argument compares V_n((1+h)B_n)-V_n(B_n) with s_n(S_n) h and lets h tend to zero.
measure_and_law_conventions.distinction: This is a total-mass formula for unnormalized surface measure, not a replacement of the probability normalization sigma_n(S_n)=1.
measure_and_law_conventions.inference_explicitly_marked: Reading 'normalized' in its usual sense gives sigma_n=s_n/s_n(S_n), hence the normalization factor n V_n(B_n). That measure-equality formula is not itself displayed on page 240.

measure_and_law_conventions.fact: For Borel measurable integrable f on R^n, 1.5 reads (n V(B))^(-1) integral_R^n f dV = integral_0^infinity r^(n-1) integral_S f(r zeta) d sigma(zeta) dr. The text attributes the constant n V(B) to sigma's normalization and suggests checking it with the indicator of B.

main_mean_value_statement.label: 1.4 Mean-Value Property
main_mean_value_statement.ambient_parameters: n > 1 under the global convention; a in R^n; r a positive ball radius as used in the section; u complex valued under the global convention.
main_mean_value_statement.hypothesis: u is harmonic on the closed ball overline(B(a,r)), interpreted by the earlier extension definition.
main_mean_value_statement.conclusion: u(a) = integral_S u(a + r zeta) d sigma(zeta).
main_mean_value_statement.integration_domain: The fixed unit sphere S; a+r zeta parametrizes the boundary of the ball centered at a. The displayed law is normalized sigma on S.
main_mean_value_statement.not_separate_hypotheses: Continuity and integrability are not separately listed in the theorem; the harmonic-extension hypothesis supplies C^2 regularity near the compact sphere.
source_proof_route: Handle n > 2 first and reduce to the unit ball by the stated normalization.
Fix epsilon in (0,1). Apply Green identity 1.1 to the annulus epsilon < |x| < 1 with v(x)=|x|^(2-n).
Use harmonic flux identity 1.3 to remove the two normal-derivative integrals.
Obtain integral_S u ds = epsilon^(1-n) integral_(epsilon S) u ds.
Rewrite this equality as integral_S u d sigma = integral_S u(epsilon zeta) d sigma(zeta).
Let epsilon tend to zero using continuity at the origin.
For n=2 use the same argument with log|x| in place of |x|^(2-n).

proof_inputs_read_directly.label: 1.1 Green identity
proof_inputs_read_directly.hypotheses: Bounded open Omega with smooth boundary; u,v C^2 on a neighborhood of its closure
proof_inputs_read_directly.formula: integral_Omega (u Delta v - v Delta u) dV = integral_boundary(Omega) (u D_n v - v D_n u) ds

proof_inputs_read_directly.label: 1.2 divergence theorem
proof_inputs_read_directly.role: The stated derivation of 1.1 uses the vector field u grad v - v grad u.

proof_inputs_read_directly.label: 1.3 harmonic flux
proof_inputs_read_directly.role: Special case of Green identity for harmonic u and v identically 1.

proof_inputs_read_directly.label: fundamental harmonic examples
proof_inputs_read_directly.role: |x|^(2-n) for n>2 and log|x| for n=2 are harmonic away from the origin; these motivate the proof's test functions.

proof_exposition_limits: The source compresses the change from ds on a scaled sphere to normalized d sigma; it does not provide a separate measure-pushforward theorem there.
The reduction to the unit ball and the limiting integral step are stated briefly, not expanded as separate lemmas.
This is an annular Green-identity proof. No Gaussian, probabilistic, heat-flow, or power-series proof of 1.4 is given on these pages.

appendix_A2_context.A1_proof_route: Split R^n as R^2 times R^(n-2), integrate slices, use planar polar coordinates to get V_n(B_n)=(2 pi/n)V_(n-2)(B_(n-2)), then induct in steps of two from V_2(B_2)=pi and V_3(B_3)=4 pi/3.
appendix_A2_context.A2_proof_route: After declaring s_n and sigma_n, use the first-order volume of a thin shell to identify s_n(S_n) with n V_n(B_n).
appendix_A2_context.encountered_A2_use_site: On printed page 241 the slice-map surface-Jacobian formula is combined with A.2 to obtain the normalized slice formula in the next theorem. That next theorem was not inspected.
appendix_A2_context.not_claimed: The source pages do not construct Hausdorff measure, prove uniqueness of orthogonally invariant probability, or present a fully formal derivation of the shell asymptotic.

pins.location: All of 1.20 and beginning of 1.17 proof

bounded_poisson_consumer.definition_1_15: P(x,zeta)=(1-|x|^2)/|x-zeta|^n. The section explicitly starts anew using this formula as the definition, so the previous derivation may be treated as motivational.
bounded_poisson_consumer.definition_1_16: For f in C(S), P[f](x)=integral_S f(zeta)P(x,zeta)d sigma(zeta), defined for x in B. The default codomain convention permits complex f.
bounded_poisson_consumer.proposition_1_18: For each zeta in S, P(.,zeta) is harmonic on R^n minus {zeta}. This is harmonicity in the first variable. The reader is asked to verify it, for example by applying the real-valued C^2 product rule 1.19 to (1-|x|^2)|x-zeta|^(-n).

proposition_1_20.a: For every x in B and zeta in S, P(x,zeta)>0.
proposition_1_20.b: For every x in B, integral_S P(x,zeta)d sigma(zeta)=1.
proposition_1_20.c: For every eta in S and every delta>0, integral over {zeta in S : |zeta-eta|>delta} of P(x,zeta)d sigma(zeta) tends to zero as x tends to eta. The surrounding domain is x in B; the limit statement does not mean evaluating the boundary singularity.

mass_one_proof_routes_as_printed: Take u identically 1 in representation formula 1.14.

To avoid using the motivational section: for x in B minus {0}, use Symmetry Lemma 1.13 to rewrite the integral as integral_S P(|x| zeta, x/|x|)d sigma(zeta). Proposition 1.18 makes this function of zeta harmonic on the closed unit ball. Apply 1.4 to obtain P(0,x/|x|)=1. Treat x=0 separately.

direct_mean_value_use_details.nonzero_condition: x/|x| is formed only after excluding x=0.
direct_mean_value_use_details.unit_direction: x/|x| is in S, so it is an admissible fixed second argument for 1.18.
direct_mean_value_use_details.radius: 0<|x|<1; the first-variable sphere |x|S lies strictly inside B.
direct_mean_value_use_details.harmonic_domain: The text expressly says the function zeta -> P(|x| zeta,x/|x|) is harmonic on the closed unit ball, rather than merely at its center.
direct_mean_value_use_details.marked_explanatory_inference: By the source formula and the dilation rule, its possible singularity as a function of zeta lies at (x/|x|)/|x|, outside the closed unit ball because |x|<1. This explains the printed closed-ball claim; it is not an independently proved new theorem here.
direct_mean_value_use_details.value_at_zero: P(0,x/|x|)=1 uses the unit norm of x/|x|; at x=0 the original kernel is identically 1 on S and sigma(S)=1.

symmetry_input.label: 1.13 Symmetry Lemma
symmetry_input.quantifiers: For every pair of nonzero x,y in R^n.
symmetry_input.printed_proof: Square both sides and expand using the Euclidean inner product.

bounded_poisson_consumer.theorem_1_17: For continuous f on S, define u as P[f] on B and f on S. Then u is continuous on the closed unit ball and harmonic on B.
theorem_1_17_proof_route: Differentiate 1.16 under the integral to obtain harmonicity from 1.18.
At eta in S, choose delta by continuity of f. Use positivity and mass one to split |u(x)-u(eta)| into near and far parts.
Bound the near part by epsilon and the far part by 2||f||_infinity times the tail mass in 1.20(c).
bounded_poisson_consumer.theorem_1_21_distinction: 1.21 later proves the representation for every u continuous on the closed ball and harmonic only on B, by 1.17 and the maximum principle. The source explicitly calls this stronger than 1.14. It is a later theorem with a different hypothesis package, not the hypothesis originally printed in 1.4.

encountered_source_use_sites_and_routes.use: Volume mean value: normalize to B, apply polar formula 1.5 to u times the indicator of B, and invoke spherical mean value 1.4. Conclusion u(a)=V(B(a,r))^(-1) integral_B(a,r) u dV under closed-ball harmonicity.

A real harmonic function vanishing at a has a zero on every sufficiently small sphere about a: the mean is zero, so the boundary restriction is either identically zero or changes sign, then connectedness supplies a zero. The real-valued qualifier is explicitly needed.
Apply 1.4 at the origin to a function harmonic on the closed unit ball to identify u(0) with its normalized spherical integral.

In the n>2 Green-identity derivation, mean value is expressly used to simplify the small-sphere contribution. Passing the remaining terms to zero yields u(x)=integral_S u(zeta)P(x,zeta)d sigma(zeta). The preceding setup assumes harmonicity on the closed unit ball and initially takes nonzero x in B.
The alternate direct proof uses the shared spherical mean-value theorem on the rescaled first-variable kernel, with x=0 handled separately.
Translations and dilations transfer the unit-ball Dirichlet results to any ball B(a,r).
A.2 converts an unnormalized surface-Jacobian formula toward a normalized spherical slice integration theorem on the next page.

source_omissions_and_review_limits: No implementation or candidate theorem names are known from this preread, and no claim of correspondence is made.
No statement in the inspected pages extends 1.4 to n=0 or n=1, non-Euclidean norms, infinite-dimensional spaces, Banach-valued codomains, or arbitrary probability laws.
The printed formula for 1.4 uses the unit sphere and an affine evaluation map; it does not state a separate theorem for an ambient sphere-restricted measure or a normalized Hausdorff measure.
No separate r=0 or r<0 case is given. Such cases would require an explicitly justified extension or a different statement.
The normalized law is characterized by Borel probability and full orthogonal invariance. The inspected source does not prove its existence or uniqueness or identify it with any library construction.
The sphere-area relation A.2 is exposed through an intuitive thin-shell argument, and the source acknowledges that some Appendix A arguments leave details to the reader.

The annular proof of 1.4 uses normalized surface measure after a compressed surface-scaling step. Its internal measure-theoretic and differentiation details are not separate source lemmas on these pages.
The alternate proof of 1.20(b) uses 1.4 plus kernel harmonicity and symmetry. The earlier representation-based proof is a second printed route; its availability does not erase the alternate route.
The two properties 'harmonic on the closed ball' and 'continuous on the closed ball and harmonic on the interior' are kept distinct by the raw text. The later theorem 1.21 treats the second package.

Not all source references or use sites in the whole book were inspected. In particular, the maximum-principle proof cited by 1.21, the source behind the polar-integration citation, and the slice theorem after page 241 are outside this coverage.
